message.abstract: <jats:p>The oxygen evolution reaction (OER) is a sluggish electrochemical semi-reaction, object of intense research for which a gold-standard electrocatalytic material is ruthenium dioxide (RuO2). It has been experimentally reported that an adsorbate with a superoxo character (-OO-H), where H is adsorbed on a lattice oxygen forming a hydrogen bond with the superoxo adsorbed on ruthenium, is preferred in place of the conventionally assumed peroxo (-OOH) one. Quantum chemical simulations addressed the origin of this outcome without taking into explicit consideration the application of oxidative voltage. In this work, we fill this gap by applying the grand canonical potential kinetic (GCP-K) methodology to study the potential dependent stability of OER key intermediates. Our results highlight an often-undermined aspect, as they show that the dynamic evolution in oxidative conditions of the RuO2 surface play a crucial role in determining the stability of the reaction intermediates. Furthermore, the results are also dependent on the environmental conditions, suggesting that by modifying the experimental conditions of nature and concentration of the supporting electrolyte, the order of stability can be reversed. Our results demonstrate major factors determining the relative stability of -OO-H compared to -OOH. These results could help future studies devoted to the understanding and rational design of novel electrocatalytic materials.</jats:p>
title: Unveiling the Stability of Oxygen Evolution Intermediates on RuO2 via Grand Canonical Density Functional Theory
